title: Ezra the Scribe
lead: Ezra, a priest of Aaron's line and a scribe of the law of Moses, came from Babylon to Jerusalem under the Persian king Artaxerxes (Ezra 7–8), led the people's confession over marriages with the peoples of the land (Ezra 9–10) and read the law to the people (Nehemiah 8). Jewish tradition calls him a second Moses; later writings make him the one who restored the Scriptures.

sections.h: Ezra in the Bible and after
sections.b:
The Bible tells Ezra's story in two places: Ezra 7–10, where he comes up from Babylon with a royal letter, a caravan and a fortune in temple gifts, and Nehemiah 8–12, where he reads the law aloud at the Water Gate and leads the celebration at the dedication of the wall. He is both priest (descended from Aaron through Zadok, Ezra 7:1–5) and scribe, a word that in the Persian court meant a trained official and in Ezra's hands came to mean a scholar of Scripture (Ezra 7:6; Ezra 7:10).

Later Jewish writers made him larger still. The Talmud says the Torah was worthy to be given through him had Moses not come first, and credits him with the square Hebrew script (Bavli Sanhedrin 21b–22a). It also lists ten enactments of Ezra, among them the public reading of the Torah on Mondays and Thursdays (Bavli Bava Kamma 82a). Irenaeus, among the church fathers, says that Ezra, inspired by God, set the words of the earlier prophets in order again after the exile (Against Heresies 3.21.2). The apocalypse called 4 Ezra (2 Esdras in many Bibles) pictures him rewriting the lost Scriptures by inspiration (4 Ezra 14). Josephus places him under Xerxes (Antiquities 11.120–158). Ben Sira's praise of famous men names Nehemiah but not Ezra (Sirach 49:13), a silence historians still discuss.
